title: Settling bets for racketeers at Lindy's
summary: Gangsters ask Greer to settle bets across from Lindy's.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: They like that, you see. They like me, because if I thought someone was right I'd come on. I didn't know the word "back". Because a lot of the times I'd be coming -- standing on Broadway and 49th Street and across the street was Lindsey's (Lindy's) a very famous -- that was the hangout for all the big gangsters in New York, Lindsey's, right at 49th and Broadway. Those racketeers would be arguing about anything. So one of them would spot me and say, "come here, Sonny, so and so . . ." Now, I don't know how they bet, but I'd kind of see my man on the side, and I'd know he'd say... I'd say, "How you going today? All you got to say is "No." I'd say no, and make my point. And here'd come a little tip of something. Nice taste.

It was beautiful. And Connie, that owned Connie's, he was always arguing. Just a horserace or something, what the hell do I know about the horses. But he'd ask me; I'd just go with him. And he would collect the bets. Stood me $20.00 or something. That was a whole lot of money then. I sneaked downtown to stand out in front of Bill (Inaudible). I know they're going to start some arguing. They called me over,

across the street. And I was settling. Like one time Sherman Billingsley Billings at the 21 Club, Sherman Billings, you had to show your birth certificate to go in. I knew this guy when he had one of them jive drugstores. There wasn't no drugs in the place but in the back he was selling/whisky--- Before he got downtown and got high class.
